chapters.s: Savitri brings together Budhba’s witness, Sonama Majhin’s offering and the children’s village game to create the first name-saving kabaddi. The new-moon ritual gives collective form to a central rule of the cycle: bodies may disappear, but a community can keep names present.
chapters.g: Chapter -82 is a central hinge in the whole Part 0 project of Water-Burial Among the Crocodiles. Here the ritual already encountered by the reader in Parts 1 and 2 as “name-saving kabaddi” is born in its first form. Savitri’s synthesis—bringing together the spirit of witness embodied by Budhba, the spirit of offering embodied by Sonama Majhin…

chapters.s: Twenty years have passed. New-moon kabaddi has become an inseparable part of village life—but in this chapter a new, human-made calamity reaches the village gate, one that no offering and no name can pacify. That night, seeing the shadow of invasion, Budhba sang a proverb-song—
chapters.g: At the beginning of the fourteenth century, the fall of the Karnata dynasty that preceded the Oiniwar line in Mithila, and incursions by the armies of the Delhi Sultanate into the Tirhut region, brought profound changes to the political structure of the area. Chapter -81 uses this historical instability as its background to show how local communal traditions, such as the kabaddi ritual…

chapters.t: The First Line of the Song
chapters.s: With the rise of the Oiniwar dynasty, a new political stability and a new literary enthusiasm are spreading through Mithila—and in this chapter, for the first time, Budhba’s story attempts to leave oral memory and descend onto the page. That day, as the first line of the song rose, the village wove a song—
chapters.g: The rule of the Oiniwar dynasty in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries is regarded as an especially important period in the history of Maithili literature, when Maithili received royal patronage and became a medium of high literary expression. The poet “Haripati” mentioned in Chapter -80 does not represent any one specific historical person…

chapters.s: Forty-five years have passed. In this chapter, for the first time, the new-moon kabaddi is played not only for the names of the dead, but also for an old wrong borne by a living person. That day, as forgiveness entered a kabaddi turn, the village sang—
chapters.g: Chapter -79 raises a difficult moral question to which there is no simple answer: is a descendant responsible for an ancestor’s wrongdoing, and if so, to what extent? The story gives no fixed theoretical answer. Raghuvir’s return of land is described not as “buying forgiveness” but as “a step toward truth,” and the matter is deliberately left incomplete.…

chapters.s: Mithila’s Panji system—which records lineage, gotra, and ancestral origin—enters the story here for the first time, bringing with it the question of which names are admitted to such records, and which are not. That day, for the names left outside the Panji, the village sang—
chapters.g: Mithila’s Panji system has long been admired among scholars for its intricate and meticulous tradition of genealogical record-keeping, but historically it was confined chiefly to the lineages of Maithil Brahmins and Karna Kayasthas. As a result, most of Mithila’s population—Shudra, Dalit, and Adivasi communities—remained outside this official system of memory.…

chapters.s: Ten years have passed. In this chapter, for the first time, Budhba himself begins to break—and the village must understand that even the one who bears witness sometimes needs a witness. That day, seeing Budhba’s silence, the village sang a proverb-song—
chapters.g: Chapter -77 gives narrative form to a psychological reality sometimes described in modern language as “compassion fatigue”: a person—or a spirit—who continuously bears the burdens of others in a one-way flow, without ever experiencing his own burden being shared, may eventually become depleted, however good his intentions.…

chapters.t: The First Lesson on a Coconut Leaf
chapters.s: Kaushalya’s daughter, Mandakini, carrying forward the knowledge of her grandmothers, brings a new idea—one that, much later, will be known as the “Coconut-Leaf School.” That day, as the children wrote their first letters on coconut leaves, they sang—
chapters.g: Chapter -76 gives narrative form to an important principle: scarcity of resources can sometimes become the mother of innovation. Where costly paper and palm-leaf manuscripts are unavailable, making education accessible through a local and readily available material—the coconut leaf—reflects practices that have, in different forms, genuinely arisen among many historically marginalized communities.…

chapters.s: The Coconut-Leaf School bore fruit in an unexpected way as well: a newly literate generation, having learned to ask questions, now begins to question its oldest tradition. That day, seeing a disciple find the courage to question the teacher, the gathering sang—
chapters.g: Chapter -75 gives narrative form to a universal social phenomenon: the tension between the rational-scientific outlook fostered by the spread of education and traditional, experience-based folk knowledge, a tension that appears in one form or another in almost every society with every generational transition. The story deliberately refuses to declare either side entirely right.…

chapters.s: The centuries-old pipal has itself grown old now—and when its leaves begin to yellow, the village realizes for the first time that Budhba’s very existence is bound to the health of this tree. That day, seeing the sickness of the tree, the old farmers sang a warning song—
chapters.g: Chapter -74 touches on a practical but serious subject: the preservation of living cultural monuments—ancient trees, historic buildings, or oral traditions—cannot be achieved through emotional reverence alone. It requires continuous, practical care, best carried out through a combination of modern knowledge, such as tree science, and traditional knowledge, such as herbal treatment.…

chapters.s: In this chapter, a melody born of grief joins the ritual and becomes the seed of the tradition that, much later, will appear as the “chapter-opening folk song.” In time, Mohan’s tradition of melodies became deeply joined to Shilavati’s ritual order, and musicians of every generation kept adding new melodies to it—for new names, new stories, new griefs, new hopes.…
chapters.g: Chapter -73 gives narrative form to a familiar human experience: the transformation of profound personal grief into artistic expression, often regarded as one of the common sources from which folk-musical traditions arise. Mohan’s melody tradition is explicitly linked here, through the “chapter-opening folk song,” to the next work (Part 1), which presents a related folk song at the beginning of each chapter.…

chapters.s: In this chapter, for the first time in many years, a marriage takes place in Garh Narikel that recalls the story of Gangesha and Malati—but this time the village responds differently. The village elders, who once could not have imagined such a marriage, accepted a new truth that night: centuries of witnessing, centuries of preserving names, and centuries of education and dialogue had, at last…
chapters.g: Chapter -72 offers a hopeful but realistic message: social change, especially in the sphere of caste-based discrimination, does not occur all at once, but results from efforts, education, dialogue, and shared experience accumulated generation after generation. The marriage of Anuradha and Gopinath, explicitly linked to the marriage of Gangesha and Malati in Chapter -91…

chapters.s: In this chapter, an epidemic engulfs Garh Narikel and the surrounding villages—and for the first time Budhba must hold so many names at once that the old method proves inadequate. From that day onward, “Collective Remembrance” became a permanent alternative within the village ritual—individual stories in ordinary times, a collective calling in times of crisis: two different forms of the same love.
chapters.g: Chapter -71 addresses a practical challenge that every tradition of preserving memory, however devoted, must eventually face: what happens when the number of the dead becomes so great that detailed individual remembrance is impossible. The development of “Collective Remembrance”—a brief communal calling in place of full individual narratives—corresponds to mourning practices that arise in societies after epidemics, wars…

chapters.s: After the epidemic, the village begins a new tradition—planting a new tree for every great remembrance. In this chapter is born the grove that, much later, will be known as “Channa Grove.” From that day onward, Channa Grove became the most sacred and important place in the village. The pipal was its heart, but all around it spread the Channa trees, each carrying its own story, its own name…
chapters.g: Chapter -70 presents the origin story of Channa Grove, the most central geographical and cultural place in Water-Burial Among the Crocodiles, Parts 1 and 2. The practice of planting a memorial tree for an important death or event exists in many cultures around the world; this chapter places that universal human impulse within the story’s particular geography.…
